title: How the internet works
examples: How does my computer find a website?
What is the difference between an IP address and a website name?
What happens to the data when I send an email?

explain.say: Today we will learn how the internet actually works for you.

items: The name becomes an IP address
Routers send packets to the destination

explain.say: First, when you visit a website, your computer needs an IP address.
Next, data is broken down into small pieces called packets for travel.
These packets travel through special devices called routers to reach their goal.
The Domain Name System or DNS translates names to numbers for you.
In real life, when you use GPS, it uses these same principles to guide you.

faq.q: What is an IP address exactly?
faq.a: An IP address is a unique string of numbers that identifies a device on the internet. It is like the street address for your computer.
asks: How do computers find each other?

faq.q: What does DNS do for me?
faq.a: DNS acts like the internet's phone book. It translates easy-to-remember website names into complex IP addresses.
asks: What is the role of DNS?

faq.q: Are packets always the same size?
faq.a: No, packets can vary in size depending on the data they carry. Routers manage these different sized pieces.
asks: Do all data bits travel together?

faq.q: What is the difference between a router and a server?
faq.a: A router directs traffic between networks, like a post office sorting mail. A server is a powerful computer that stores and sends out the website data.
asks: What is the job of a router?
Is a server a type of router?

faq.q: Do I need to know my IP address to use the internet?
faq.a: Yes, your network needs an IP address to send and receive data packets correctly. This is how the internet knows where to send things.
asks: Can I browse without an IP?
Is an IP address necessary for connection?

facts: An IP address is a numerical label assigned to every device connected to a network.
DNS translates human-readable domain names into machine-readable IP addresses.
Data sent over the internet is broken into small units called packets for efficient routing.
Routers examine the destination IP address on each packet to forward it correctly.

quiz.say: If you type www.school.edu, what system finds the correct number?
quiz.why: The DNS system is specifically designed to translate names like www.school.edu into IP addresses.

wrong.0: Routers only know how to send data using numbers, not names.
wrong.1: Packets are the pieces of data, not the translation service itself.
wrong.2: The IP address is the result of the lookup, not the service that performs it.

quiz.say: When sending a large photo, what is the data usually split into?
quiz.why: Breaking data into smaller packets helps manage transmission and allows for error checking.

wrong.0: Bits are the smallest unit, but packets are the organized groups of bits sent across the network.
wrong.1: Bytes are a measure of data size, but packets describe the unit of transmission.
wrong.2: A stream suggests continuous flow, but the internet handles data in discrete, manageable packets.

quiz.say: A device that reads the destination IP address to send data is a:
quiz.why: Routers are specialized networking devices whose main job is directing packets between different networks.

wrong.0: DNS only provides the address; it does not physically move the data packets.
wrong.2: A server provides the data, but it does not direct the path of the incoming packets.
wrong.3: A client is the device requesting the data, not the device directing it.
